balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For ASX Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For ASX Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For ASX Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For ASX Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For ASX Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For ASX Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For ASX Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For ASX Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For ASX Limited: this is a blend of listing fees, trading/clearing/settlement fees and technology & data fees across four reporting segments -- see the Segment Revenue Mix chart below for what is actually driving the growth rate.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic (volumes, listings) or fee-rate driven
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue mix
segmentRevenue.content:
ASX reports four segments: Listings (fees for admitting and retaining issuers), Markets (cash equities and futures trading/clearing), Securities & Payments (settlement, registry and payments infrastructure, including CHESS), and Technology & Data (connectivity, data and technical services sold to market participants).

For ASX Limited: Markets is the most cyclical of the four -- it scales with cash-market and derivatives trading activity -- while Technology & Data and Securities & Payments are closer to recurring, subscription-like revenue. A widening Markets share signals a more volume-sensitive earnings mix; a widening Technology & Data share signals a more annuity-like one. Only disclosed from FY2024 onward.

What to watch:

  • Which segment is driving total revenue growth in a given year
  • Markets segment revenue against the Cash Market Trades & Futures Contracts chart -- it should track volumes, not just fee rates
  • Technology & Data growth as a proxy for CHESS replacement and data-product monetisation progress

marketActivity.title: Market activity volumes
marketActivity.content:
Cash market trades and futures contracts are the number of transactions ASX's markets and clearing houses processed in the year (in thousands); new listings is the count of new entities admitted to the exchange.

For ASX Limited: these are ASX's own disclosed operating volumes, not line items on the income statement or balance sheet -- they are the throughput that the Markets segment's per-trade and per-contract fees are levied on, and a leading indicator for that segment's revenue a period or two ahead of the P&L. New listings (and the shrinking Listed Entities count, not charted here) is the IPO-pipeline health check behind the Listings segment.

What to watch:

  • Trade/contract volumes diverging from Markets segment revenue (fee-rate or mix changes)
  • New listings trending against delistings -- ASX's listed-entity count has been declining most years in this series
  • Futures volumes as the more resilient of the two in down markets, since cash-equity turnover is more sentiment-driven

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For ASX Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
